notes: PSA 31 ng/mL. PI-RADS 5. PSAD 0.95. Prostate volume 33 mL. csPCa 0.93.

note_sections.t: Multidisciplinary consultation required to determine definitive management strategy following confirmation of high-grade prostate adenocarcinoma and rapid PSA progression.

This 63-year-old retired police officer is referred for treatment decision-making after a biopsy-proven diagnosis of prostate cancer. His PSA has escalated dramatically from 3.1 ng/mL in February 2022 to 18.8 ng/mL in August 2023, and most recently to 31.0 ng/mL in January 2025. He reports moderate lower urinary tract symptoms, quantified by an IPSS score of 16, which has been stable over the past year. He is divorced but lives with a partner, and his adult son serves as his primary contact for medical matters. Socially, he consumes approximately two units of alcohol per week and maintains a daily walking routine of 20 minutes. He is an ex-smoker with a 23 pack-year history, having quit in 2008. Recent non-urological reviews include a stable cardiology assessment in autumn 2024, a surveillance colonoscopy, and a baseline screening at the memory clinic. He has no recorded comorbidities and takes no regular medication, though he has a known penicillin allergy causing a rash.

Per rectum, the prostate feels symmetrically enlarged but without discrete nodules or asymmetry, consistent with a clinical stage of cT1c. The general examination is unremarkable, with stable vital signs including a blood pressure of 134/68 mmHg and a heart rate of 61 bpm. There is no palpable lymphadenopathy or organomegaly on abdominal examination.

living: Lives with partner; adult children visit weekly
